issues.legal_issue: Participation in a fatal assault cannot be treated as proved beyond reasonable doubt when the medical evidence conflicts with the eyewitness account of the alleged weapons and the remaining evidence is insufficient.
material_facts: Witnesses attributed attacks with sickles to two accused and attacks with axes to the other two.
The medical evidence indicated that the deceased's injuries could have been caused by the back portions of axes rather than by sickles.
The medical officer's evidence supported the possibility that the incised injuries were caused by a hard and sharp substance such as an axe.
The court considered the evidence against the two accused said to have used sickles feeble and insufficient to prove their participation beyond reasonable doubt.
issues.conclusion: The convictions and sentences of the two accused alleged to have used sickles were set aside, and they were acquitted because their guilt had not been established beyond reasonable doubt.
issues.legal_principle: The prosecution must establish an accused's guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Here, the discrepancy between the eyewitness account and medical evidence, together with the insufficiency of the evidence of participation, left reasonable doubt. The court set aside convictions under Section 304, Part I, of the Indian Penal Code; no earlier cases are cited.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The matter is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.eyewitness_weapon_account_conflicts_with: Eyewitnesses describe a weapon or manner of attack that the medical evidence does not support.
predicates.evidence_of_accused_participation_is_ins: The evidence identifying the accused as a participant is too weak to establish participation beyond reasonable doubt.

issues.definition: When a criminal conviction is appealed, the eyewitness account conflicts with the medical evidence, and the evidence of the accused's participation is insufficient, the accused is acquitted for failure of proof.

issues.legal_issue: An accused who participates in a fatal attack while acting in defence of another person or property is liable when the force used exceeds the right of private defence.
material_facts: The two accused who remained convicted were found to have participated in the occurrence and attacked the deceased with axes.
The first accused, their father, had a minor injury to his finger, and the court accepted that the deceased had bitten it.
The attack occurred during a dispute over crops and possession of land.
The court agreed that the two accused had exceeded the right of private defence of their father's body and of property.
issues.conclusion: The convictions of the two accused under Section 304, Part I, of the Indian Penal Code and their five-year prison sentences were retained.
issues.legal_principle: The right of private defence of the body and property does not justify force that exceeds that right. The court applied that principle and retained the convictions under Section 304, Part I, of the Indian Penal Code. No earlier cases are cited.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction_after_st: The matter is an appeal from a conviction entered after the prosecution appealed an acquittal.
predicates.accused_participated_in_fatal_attack: The accused took part in an attack that caused the victim's death.
predicates.attack_occurred_in_defence_of_person_or_: The accused acted in response to an asserted threat to a person or property.
predicates.defensive_force_was_excessive: The force used in response went beyond the scope of the asserted defensive right.

issues.definition: When an accused appeals a conviction entered after a prosecution appeal against acquittal, participated in a fatal attack while acting in defence of a person or property, and used excessive defensive force, the conviction for culpable homicide is retained.
